sla_notes_intro: Literature is imaginative writing and oral art that expresses human experience through language.
sla_notes_details: Literature includes stories, poems, plays and other artistic uses of words. Its functions are to entertain, educate, preserve culture and history, criticise society, develop language and imagination, and help people understand themselves and others. It can be oral or written and is grouped in three main genres: prose, poetry and drama.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a folktale entertains children while teaching honesty, and a poem may criticise corruption while entertaining the reader.
sla_notes_daily_life: People enjoy literature in songs, stories, films, theatre and poems, and learn values from it in everyday life.
sla_exercise: Define literature.::Imaginative writing or oral art that expresses human experience through language.||Name the three main genres of literature.::Prose, poetry and drama.||State two functions of literature.::To entertain and to educate.

sla_notes_intro: Oral literature is passed by word of mouth, while written literature is recorded in writing.
sla_notes_details: Oral literature includes folktales, songs, riddles, proverbs, fables, myths, legends and poems, and it depends on performance, memory and audience participation. Written literature includes novels, short stories, poems and plays that exist in written or printed form. Oral literature changes as it is retold, while written literature is usually fixed. Both preserve culture and values, and many written works come from oral traditions.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, the proverb 'Haba na haba hujaza kibaba' is oral literature, while a published novel is written literature.
sla_notes_daily_life: Grandparents telling stories at night and children reciting riddles are everyday examples of oral literature.
sla_exercise: Differentiate oral from written literature.::Oral literature is spoken and passed down by word of mouth; written literature is recorded in writing.||Give two forms of oral literature.::Riddles and proverbs.||Why does oral literature change over time?::Because it is retold from memory by different people.

sla_notes_intro: Oral forms reflect the experiences, beliefs and values of the community that creates them.
sla_notes_details: Folktales teach moral lessons through characters such as clever hares or greedy people; songs express joy, work, love and mourning; riddles test thinking; proverbs state wisdom in short sayings; fables use animals to represent human behaviour and idioms use figurative language to express ideas. Students connect these forms to real experiences, such as honesty, hard work, cooperation and respect.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, the fable of a hare who tricks bigger animals can be related to how a weak person may use wisdom to overcome difficulties.
sla_notes_daily_life: Proverbs and stories are used in families, schools and communities to give advice and guide behaviour.
sla_exercise: What is a fable?::A short story, usually with animals as characters, that teaches a moral lesson.||Give an example of an idiom.::'To kick the bucket' meaning to die.||How do proverbs help society?::They give short pieces of wisdom that guide behaviour.

sla_notes_intro: Characters are the people or figures in a story, and their actions and attitudes drive the plot and reveal themes.
sla_notes_details: Readers examine what characters do, say and think, how they treat others and how they respond to problems. Characters may be round (complex and changing), flat (simple), protagonists or antagonists. Students reflect on whether the characters' choices are wise and how they relate to real life, using evidence from the text.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a character who helps neighbours despite poverty shows generosity, while a character who cheats to succeed shows greed and may face consequences.
sla_notes_daily_life: Reflecting on characters helps readers understand people around them and make good choices.
sla_exercise: Differentiate a protagonist from an antagonist.::The protagonist is the main character; the antagonist opposes the protagonist.||How can a reader learn about a character's attitude?::From what the character says, does and thinks.||Name one type of character.::Round character (or flat character).

sla_notes_intro: Multiculturalism is the presence and respect of many cultures in a society, while self-consciousness is awareness of one's own identity and values.
sla_notes_details: Literary works depict people from different cultures, languages and beliefs and may show conflict or harmony between them. Reading about other cultures develops tolerance, respect and understanding, and comparing them with one's own culture strengthens self-awareness.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a novel about a boy who moves from a village to a city may show differences in food, language and customs.
sla_notes_daily_life: Tanzania has many ethnic groups and languages, so appreciation of multiculturalism promotes peace and unity.
sla_exercise: What is multiculturalism?::The existence of many cultures within a society and respect for them.||How does literature promote tolerance?::It presents other people's lives and cultures so that readers understand them.||What is self-consciousness in literature?::Awareness of one's own identity and values.

sla_notes_intro: Readers compare the cultural values shown in a novel with their own to understand similarities and differences.
sla_notes_details: Values such as respect for elders, hospitality, honesty, community, gender roles, marriage and education may be depicted. Students identify the values shown, discuss whether they are similar to their own, and justify their opinions with evidence from the text and respect for differing views.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a novel that shows respect for elders through greetings may be compared with how young people greet elders in one's own community.
sla_notes_daily_life: Reflection helps young people appreciate their culture and accept differences.
sla_exercise: Give two cultural values that may be found in a novel.::Respect for elders and hospitality.||Why compare a novel's values with your own?::To understand similarities and differences between cultures.||How should you support your opinion about a value?::With evidence from the text.

sla_notes_intro: Character development is the way a character changes or is revealed as the story progresses.
sla_notes_details: A protagonist may grow in wisdom, courage or morality or may fail because of flaws. An antagonist may be a person, group or force that creates conflict. Students trace events that shape each character, the motives behind their actions and the outcome, and assess how the writer makes them believable.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a protagonist who begins as fearful and learns courage after facing challenges shows positive development.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding character growth helps learners think about how experiences shape real people.
sla_exercise: What is character development?::How a character changes or is revealed over the course of a story.||Can an antagonist be a force rather than a person?::Yes, for example poverty or nature.||Give one way a writer shows a character's development.::Through the character's actions and choices over time.

sla_notes_intro: Values are beliefs about what is good, perspectives are ways of viewing things and identities describe who a person or group is.
sla_notes_details: In literature, characters have values (honesty, loyalty, courage), perspectives shaped by age, gender, culture and experience, and identities linked to family, community, gender or nation. Understanding these concepts helps readers interpret why characters behave as they do.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, two characters may view land differently: one as a family inheritance and another as a commodity to sell.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding perspectives helps people respect others and resolve disagreements.
sla_exercise: Define value.::A belief about what is important or good.||What is perspective?::A way of viewing or understanding something.||Name one factor that shapes identity.::Culture (or family, gender, nationality).

sla_notes_intro: Readers compare characters' views and values with their own to judge and learn from them.
sla_notes_details: Students identify a character's perspective, explain the reasons behind it using evidence in the text, and compare it with their own values, saying where they agree and disagree and why. Respectful discussion and evidence-based reasoning are emphasised.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a character who believes that girls do not need education can be compared with the reader's belief in equal opportunity.
sla_notes_daily_life: Comparing perspectives builds empathy and critical thinking, which are useful in family and community discussions.

sla_notes_intro: Narrative techniques are the methods writers use to tell a story, and stylistic devices are the language tools they use to create effects.
sla_notes_details: Narrative techniques include point of view, flashback, foreshadowing, dialogue, narration, setting, symbolism and suspense. Stylistic devices include simile, metaphor, personification, imagery, hyperbole, irony, alliteration and repetition. Students identify these in texts and explain their effect on meaning.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, 'her smile was the sunrise' is a metaphor that shows joy, and a flashback reveals a character's past to explain present actions.
sla_notes_daily_life: These devices appear in songs, advertisements, speeches and everyday speech.
sla_exercise: Give two narrative techniques.::Flashback and dialogue (or foreshadowing, point of view).||Identify the device in 'the wind whispered'.::Personification.||What is the effect of a simile?::It compares two things to make a description clearer or more vivid.

sla_notes_intro: Narrative and stylistic techniques give a novel its meaning, beauty and emotional effect.
sla_notes_details: Point of view controls what the reader knows; foreshadowing builds suspense; flashback explains motives; imagery creates pictures in the mind; irony reveals contradictions; symbolism gives deeper meanings. Students explain why the writer chose these devices and what they add to the message of the text.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a dark, stormy setting may foreshadow a tragedy and prepare the reader for it.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding writers' techniques improves reading, writing and speaking skills.
sla_exercise: What does foreshadowing do?::It hints at events that will happen later.||Why do writers use imagery?::To create pictures in the reader's mind.||What is symbolism?::Using an object or action to represent a deeper idea.

sla_notes_intro: Some literary devices are used to create particular feelings such as fear, pity, joy or anger in the reader.
sla_notes_details: Devices include imagery, tone, mood, dramatic irony, suspense, exaggeration, repetition and emotive language. A writer may use vivid description of suffering to create pity, or fast pacing to create excitement. Students identify these devices and explain how they influence emotions.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, describing a hungry child's thin hands can evoke sympathy in the reader.
sla_notes_daily_life: Emotional writing is used in stories, songs, speeches and campaigns to influence audiences.
sla_exercise: What is mood in a story?::The feeling or atmosphere created for the reader.||Give one device that creates suspense.::Foreshadowing (or delayed information).||Why do writers use emotive language?::To make readers feel strongly about a subject.

sla_notes_intro: Critical reading involves several thinking skills that help readers understand a text.
sla_notes_details: Observation is noticing details in the text; analysis is breaking the text into parts and studying them; inference is drawing conclusions from clues; communication is expressing ideas clearly in discussion and writing; problem-solving is identifying characters' problems and suggesting solutions. Together they help readers interpret literature deeply.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, noticing that a character avoids eye contact (observation) may lead to the inference that he is hiding something.
sla_notes_daily_life: These skills are useful in all subjects and in solving problems in daily life.
sla_exercise: What is inference?::A conclusion drawn from clues or evidence.||Give one critical thinking skill used in reading.::Analysis (or observation, inference).||Why is communication important in literature study?::To share and justify interpretations.

sla_notes_intro: Relationships among characters shape the plot and reveal the themes of a novel.
sla_notes_details: Relationships may be family, friendship, love, rivalry, leader and follower or employer and employee. They may be supportive or conflicting. Students explain how relationships develop and how they affect the characters' choices and the story's outcome.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a friendship between two characters may help one to overcome hardship, while rivalry between brothers may lead to conflict.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding relationships in stories helps readers understand real-life relationships.
sla_exercise: Give two types of relationship between characters.::Friendship and rivalry.||How can relationships affect the plot?::They create conflicts or support that move the story forward.||Why study relationships between characters?::To understand motives and themes.

sla_notes_intro: Characters' choices lead to consequences from which readers can learn lessons.
sla_notes_details: Students examine decisions made by characters, the reasons behind them, their results and what they teach about honesty, greed, courage, responsibility or patience. They discuss whether the decisions were wise and what they would do in the same situation.

sla_notes_daily_life: Lessons from stories help young people make wise decisions in life.

sla_notes_intro: A theme is the central idea or message that a work of literature explores.
sla_notes_details: Common themes include love, poverty, corruption, education, power, gender, family, identity, justice, betrayal and hope. Themes are identified from the plot, characters, conflicts and title, and are supported by examples. A novel may have a major theme and several minor themes.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, in a story where a poor family struggles to pay school fees, poverty and the value of education are themes.
sla_notes_daily_life: Themes in literature reflect real problems in society such as unemployment and inequality.
sla_exercise: Define theme.::The central idea or message in a literary work.||Name two common themes in literature.::Love and corruption.||How do you identify a theme?::By studying the plot, characters, conflicts and title.

sla_notes_intro: Corruption and bribery are social themes that writers often use to criticise abuse of power.
sla_notes_details: Corruption is the abuse of power for personal gain, and bribery is giving or receiving something of value to influence a decision. Students analyse how these themes are shown through characters, events and outcomes, their causes such as greed and weak systems, effects such as injustice and poverty, and possible solutions like honesty and strong laws.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, an official who demands money before offering a service shows corruption and its impact on ordinary citizens.
sla_notes_daily_life: Learning about corruption helps citizens reject bribery and support transparency in their communities.
sla_exercise: Define bribery.::Giving or receiving something of value to influence a decision unfairly.||Give one effect of corruption on society.::Injustice (or poverty, loss of trust).||Suggest one solution to corruption.::Honesty and strict enforcement of laws.

sla_notes_details: Students explain why characters act the way they do given their circumstances, such as poverty, tradition or pressure, and how these actions bring out themes. They justify their explanations using evidence and logical reasoning.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a character who lies to protect a family member reflects the theme of loyalty in a difficult context.
sla_notes_daily_life: Considering context helps people judge actions fairly in real life.

sla_notes_intro: The title of a novel often points to its main idea, symbol or message.
sla_notes_details: A title may name a character, a place, an object or a key idea. Students study how the title connects to the events and themes, and what it suggests about the writer's message. Some titles are literal while others are symbolic or ironical.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a novel titled 'The Broken Bridge' may symbolise damaged relationships in a community.
sla_notes_daily_life: Reading titles carefully helps in understanding the main idea of books, films and news stories.

sla_notes_intro: A novel is relevant when its issues and lessons relate to the reader's own community and time.
sla_notes_details: Students discuss how issues such as poverty, corruption, gender roles, education, health or family conflict in the novel appear in their society, and what lessons the novel offers. They give reasons and examples and suggest how the community can use those lessons.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a novel about child marriage is relevant in communities where the practice still occurs.
sla_notes_daily_life: Relating literature to society encourages readers to take part in solving social problems.

sla_notes_intro: Poetry is a form of literature that uses rhythm, imagery and condensed language to express feelings and ideas.
sla_notes_details: Forms of poetry include lyric, narrative, ballad, elegy, ode, sonnet, free verse and haiku. Poetic features include stanza, line, rhyme, rhythm, repetition and imagery. Figurative language includes simile, metaphor, personification, hyperbole, symbolism and irony, which give words meanings beyond the literal.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, in 'Time is a thief', a metaphor compares time to a thief because it steals moments from our lives.
sla_notes_daily_life: Poetry is heard in songs, wedding chants, praise poems and slogans.
sla_exercise: What is a stanza?::A group of lines in a poem.||Give two forms of poetry.::Elegy and sonnet (or ballad, ode, free verse).||Identify the figure of speech in 'as brave as a lion'.::Simile.

sla_notes_details: Students read poems and identify the main ideas by studying the title, the speaker, the images and the tone. They explain how the poet develops the theme through stanzas, imagery and other devices and link the theme to real life.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a poem describing a farmer's struggle in drought may portray the theme of hardship and perseverance.

sla_notes_intro: Composing a poem is the creative process of using words, imagery and sound to express an idea.
sla_notes_details: Steps: choose a topic and audience, decide on the message, choose a form, use imagery and figurative language, arrange lines and stanzas, consider rhythm and rhyme, and revise the draft. Students share poems with classmates for feedback.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a poem about rainfall may use images such as 'silver threads from the sky' to show the beauty of rain.
sla_notes_daily_life: Poem writing develops creativity and can be used in songs, cards, speeches and celebrations.

sla_assessment_criteria: The concepts of antithesis, anticlimax, paradox, irony, unreliable narrator and suspense are well explained.

sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: These are literary concepts that create contrast, surprise and uncertainty in works of art.
sla_notes_details: Antithesis places opposite ideas together for contrast ('to err is human, to forgive divine'). Anticlimax is a sudden drop from something serious to something trivial. A paradox is a statement that seems contradictory but contains truth. Irony is a difference between what is expected and what happens. An unreliable narrator tells a story that cannot be fully trusted. Suspense keeps the audience uncertain about what will happen.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, 'the more you learn, the less you know' is a paradox that suggests knowledge reveals how much is still unknown.
sla_notes_daily_life: These concepts appear in films, jokes, plays, speeches and everyday storytelling.
sla_exercise: Define irony.::A difference between what is expected and what actually happens.||What is a paradox?::A statement that seems contradictory but reveals a truth.||What is suspense?::A feeling of uncertainty and excitement about what will happen next.

sla_notes_details: Students examine how the title connects to characters, events and themes, and whether it is literal, symbolic or ironic. They also discuss what it makes the audience expect before watching or reading.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a play titled 'The Feast' might deal with a celebration that leads to conflict.
sla_notes_daily_life: Titles in theatre and films attract audiences and communicate the main idea.
sla_exercise: What does a title tell about a play?::Its subject, conflict or main message.||Give one type of title.::Ironic title (or symbolic, literal).||Why do writers choose titles carefully?::To attract attention and suggest the message.

sla_notes_intro: An ironical title suggests the opposite of what happens in the play, creating deeper meaning.
sla_notes_details: For example, a play called 'A Happy Home' that shows conflict and suffering uses irony to criticise or highlight a problem. Ironical titles make the audience think, create humour or criticism and emphasise the difference between appearance and reality.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, 'The Honest Man' as a title of a play about a corrupt official is ironical.
sla_notes_daily_life: Irony in titles is used in newspapers, films and songs to attract attention and to criticise.
sla_exercise: What is an ironical title?::A title that suggests the opposite of what really happens.||What effect does an ironical title have?::It makes the audience think and emphasises the contrast.||Give an example of an ironical title.::'The Honest Man' for a play about a corrupt official.

sla_notes_intro: Creativity is the ability to produce original ideas, and visualization is the ability to form pictures in the mind to guide writing.
sla_notes_details: Writers visualize settings, characters and events before writing and use sensory details (sight, sound, smell, taste, touch) to make writing vivid. Creativity is encouraged by observing, reading widely, brainstorming, asking 'what if' questions and using personal experience.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a writer imagines a busy market with the smell of spices and noisy traders before writing a scene.
sla_notes_daily_life: Creative thinking is useful in advertising, design, storytelling and problem solving.
sla_exercise: Define visualization.::Forming pictures in the mind to guide writing.||Name one way to develop creativity.::Reading widely (or brainstorming, observing).||Why use sensory details?::To make writing vivid and realistic.

sla_notes_intro: Planning helps a writer organise ideas before composing a poem.
sla_notes_details: Steps: decide the topic and message; choose the form (free verse, rhyming poem); brainstorm words, images and figures of speech; consider rhyme and rhythm; and outline the stanzas. Planning reduces confusion and makes the poem more focused.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a plan for a poem about friendship lists images such as 'a bridge', words that rhyme and the number of stanzas.
sla_notes_daily_life: Planning is useful in speech writing, song writing and all creative work.
sla_exercise: Why plan a poem?::To organise ideas and make the poem focused.||Name two things to decide in the plan.::Topic and form.||What is rhythm?::The pattern of beats or sounds in a poem.

sla_notes_details: The writer produces a draft with stanzas and lines, applies figurative language, checks rhyme and rhythm, chooses words carefully, revises for meaning and flow, edits grammar and spelling and produces a final copy. Peer review helps to improve the poem.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a student's poem about the sea uses a metaphor 'the sea is a giant heart' and repetition to give rhythm.

sla_notes_intro: A play explores themes through dialogue, action and conflict performed on stage.
sla_notes_details: Students identify themes such as power, greed, love, justice, tradition versus change, poverty and family loyalty. They support each theme with events, speeches and characters' actions, and explain how the playwright develops it across acts and scenes.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a play in which a ruler ignores his people's suffering may explore the theme of abuse of power.
sla_notes_daily_life: Themes in plays can be seen in school drama, radio plays and television dramas that address social issues.

sla_notes_intro: Conflict is the struggle between opposing forces that drives the plot of a play.
sla_notes_details: Types include internal conflict (within a character), conflict between characters, conflict between an individual and society, and conflict with nature or fate. Students identify the cause, development, climax and resolution of the conflicts and discuss their effects on characters.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a young man torn between duty to his family and his personal dream faces an internal conflict.
sla_notes_daily_life: Conflicts in drama mirror real conflicts in families, workplaces and communities.
sla_exercise: Name two types of conflict in drama.::Internal conflict and conflict between characters.||What is the climax?::The turning point or most intense moment of a plot.||Why is conflict important in a play?::It creates tension and moves the plot forward.

sla_notes_intro: Readers connect their own life experiences to the themes of a play to understand it more deeply.
sla_notes_details: Students identify a theme, recall similar experiences from their families or communities, and discuss how the play's message can guide them. They use evidence from the play and maintain respect for others' experiences.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a play about peer pressure can be related to a student's experience of being encouraged to skip school.

sla_notes_intro: Motivation is the reason that leads a character to act in a particular way.
sla_notes_details: Motives may be love, fear, revenge, ambition, greed, duty or survival. Students study the characters' words and actions, infer their motives and discuss whether the choices were justified and what happened as a result.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a character who breaks the law to feed a hungry family is motivated by love and desperation.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding motives helps people judge actions fairly and find better solutions.
sla_exercise: Define motivation.::The reason that makes a character act in a certain way.||Give two possible motives of characters.::Love and greed (or fear, revenge).||How can a motive be inferred?::From the character's words, actions and circumstances.

sla_notes_intro: Plays highlight social problems, and readers can suggest practical solutions to them.
sla_notes_details: Students identify challenges such as poverty, corruption, discrimination, lack of education or conflict, discuss their causes and effects, and suggest realistic solutions, such as dialogue, education, fair laws and cooperation. They justify their suggestions with reasoning.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, to solve a conflict between two villages over water, the play may suggest sharing resources and mediating through elders.

sla_notes_intro: A play is made up of elements that work together to tell a story on stage.
sla_notes_details: Characters are the people who act; plot is the sequence of events; setting is the time and place; stage directions are the playwright's instructions about movement, tone, lighting and props; spectacle refers to the visual elements such as costumes, scenery and lighting. Together they create the performance.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a stage direction such as '(She looks away, angry)' guides the actor's expression and movement.
sla_notes_daily_life: These elements are used in school drama, church performances and television plays.
sla_exercise: What is a stage direction?::An instruction from the playwright about how a play should be performed.||Define setting.::The time and place in which the action takes place.||What is spectacle?::The visual elements of a play, such as costumes and scenery.

sla_notes_intro: The plot of a play develops through stages that build and release tension.
sla_notes_details: The stages are exposition (introduction of characters and setting), rising action (development of conflict), climax (turning point), falling action (events after the climax) and resolution or denouement (ending). Students identify these stages in a play and explain how each contributes to the story.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a play begins by introducing a village family (exposition), then a land dispute grows (rising action), a confrontation occurs (climax) and a settlement follows (resolution).
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding plot structure helps in writing and analysing stories, films and speeches.
sla_exercise: List the five stages of plot development.::Exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution.||What happens at the climax?::The conflict reaches its highest point or turning point.||What is the resolution?::The ending in which the conflict is settled.

sla_notes_intro: A play is composed by writing dialogue and stage directions organised into acts and scenes.
sla_notes_details: Steps include choosing a theme, developing characters, planning the plot, deciding the setting, writing dialogue with speaker names, adding stage directions, dividing the play into two acts and scenes, and revising. Dialogue should reveal character, advance the plot and sound natural.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, in Act One a young girl is denied school fees and in Act Two she finds support from her community.
sla_notes_daily_life: Writing plays develops language, teamwork and creativity, and they can be performed in schools.
sla_exercise: What is an act?::A major division of a play.||Why do plays include stage directions?::To guide actors and directors on how to perform.||What should dialogue do?::Reveal character and move the plot forward.

sla_notes_intro: Irony creates contrast between what is said or expected and what actually occurs.
sla_notes_details: Dramatic irony occurs when the audience knows something the characters do not. Situational irony occurs when the outcome is the opposite of what is expected. Students identify examples in plays and explain how they create humour, tension or criticism.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, the audience knows that a friend is a traitor while the hero trusts him, which is dramatic irony and builds tension.
sla_notes_daily_life: Irony appears in films, comedies and everyday events when things turn out differently from expectation.
sla_exercise: Define dramatic irony.::When the audience knows something that the characters do not.||What is situational irony?::When the result is the opposite of what is expected.||Why do playwrights use irony?::To create tension, humour or criticism.

sla_notes_intro: Suspense keeps the audience curious and anxious about what will happen next.
sla_notes_details: Playwrights create suspense by delaying information, giving clues, using foreshadowing, pauses, sound and lighting, and ending scenes with unanswered questions. Students judge how effective suspense is in holding attention and developing the plot.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a knock at the door at midnight, with no reply from the characters, makes the audience wonder who is there.
sla_notes_daily_life: Suspense is used in movies, news headlines and storytelling to keep people interested.
sla_exercise: What is suspense?::A feeling of uncertainty and excitement about what will happen.||Give one way to create suspense.::Delay important information (or use foreshadowing).||Why is suspense effective?::It keeps the audience engaged.

sla_notes_intro: Antithesis presents opposing ideas together, which can create ambiguity or double meanings.
sla_notes_details: In plays, antithesis may appear in characters (good against evil), speeches ('love and hate') or situations (wealth and poverty). It can leave the audience uncertain about who is right or what will occur, encouraging deeper thinking. Students explain how the technique shapes meaning and effect.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a character who is both kind and cruel makes the audience unsure whether to trust him.
sla_notes_daily_life: Ambiguity in literature encourages readers to think and to look at issues from more than one side.
sla_exercise: Define antithesis.::The placing of contrasting ideas together.||How can antithesis create ambiguity?::It makes it unclear which side is right or how events will end.||Give one example of antithesis.::Love and hate (or rich and poor).

learning_activity_name: Make a plan for composing a play (plot, setting, characterisation and stage direction)
sla_name: Planning to compose a play
sla_assessment_criteria: A plan for composing a play is correctly made.
sla_teaching_aids: Selected literary texts|ICT tools|Audio/ audio-visual materials
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Planning a play organises the story, characters and setting before writing.
sla_notes_details: The plan includes the theme, the plot outline (stages), the setting, a list of characters with traits, the conflict, the number of acts and scenes, and the stage directions needed. A good plan makes writing easier and the play more coherent.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a plan for a play about environmental care lists characters (farmer, elder, student), setting (village), conflict (tree cutting) and the resolution (tree planting).
sla_notes_daily_life: Planning is useful for writing scripts for radio, television and school events.
sla_exercise: Name two things to include in a play plan.::The plot and the characters.||Why is planning important?::It makes the play organised and coherent.||What is characterisation?::How the writer creates and presents characters.

learning_activity_name: Apply literary skills to compose a two-acts play
sla_name: Applying literary skills to compose a two-act play (Form IV)
sla_assessment_criteria: Literary skills for composing a two-acts play are correctly applied.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Selected novels, plays and poems|Manila paper
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Students write the full script of a two-act play using their plan and literary techniques.
sla_notes_details: The script contains a title, a list of characters, act and scene divisions, dialogue, stage directions and a clear plot with conflict, climax and resolution. Techniques such as irony, suspense and symbolism are applied. The script is revised, edited and presented for feedback or performance.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a student's script includes a scene where two characters argue about land and a stage direction that shows one leaving the stage angrily.
sla_notes_daily_life: Play writing helps in preparing scripts for school events and community drama for social messages.
sla_exercise: What should a play script include?::Title, characters, acts, dialogue and stage directions.||Why revise a script?::To improve clarity, coherence and effect.||Name one technique to include in a play.::Suspense (or irony, symbolism).

sla_name: Using ICT tools and digital platforms to write and publish a play
sla_method: Skills lab and ICT tools Publishing
sla_assessment_criteria: ICT tools and digital platforms are appropriately applied in writing and publishing a play.
sla_teaching_aids: Textbook|Selected novels, plays and poems|Manila paper
sla_references: TET(2023), LITERATURE IN ENGLISH SYLLABUS FOR ORDINARY SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Digital tools help students write, edit, record and share their plays.
sla_notes_details: Scripts can be typed in word processors, edited collaboratively, recorded on a phone as audio or video, and shared through school websites, blogs or social media. Learners follow copyright and safe online practice.
sla_notes_illustrations: For example, a class records their play on a phone and shares it on the school's online platform.
sla_notes_daily_life: Digital publishing helps students reach wider audiences with creative work.
sla_exercise: Name one ICT tool for writing a play.::Word processor.||How can a play be shared online?::By posting a recording on a website or blog.||Why follow copyright when publishing?::To respect the rights of the original creators.
